transcript.text: Water started coming into my basement last night after the storm. I don't know who to call.

I'm sorry, that's a stressful thing to wake up to. Water coming in after a storm is usually a job for a water damage restoration company first. They pump the water out and dry everything so you don't end up with mold. Fixing why it got in comes after that.

Safety first: if the water is anywhere near outlets, extension cords, appliances or your electrical panel, stay out of it. If you can't safely reach the panel, call your electric utility to cut the power.

Two quick questions so I can find someone near you:
1. What's your ZIP code?
2. How much water is there? For example, a damp corner, about an inch across the floor, or deeper? And is it still coming in?

It's 94087. There's about 2 inches across the whole basement floor, coming in along the back wall, and it's still seeping a little but slower now. Nothing electrical is underwater as far as I can tell.

Good that nothing electrical is in the water. With 2 inches across the whole floor and water still seeping in, it's worth getting someone out today. Here are the best matches near Sunnyvale:

1. Clearway Restoration: 408-457-0826. The closest at about 5.8 km away in Santa Clara, and they advertise 24/7 emergency service. This is my top pick.
2. Servpro: 650-770-2992. About 6.6 km away in Sunnyvale and a well-known restoration company, though their listing doesn't show 24/7 hours.
3. Reactic Restoration: 408-998-4840. Also 24/7, but farther away, about 11.4 km in San Jose.

my furnace stopped working and the house is getting really cold

That's no fun, especially when it's cold out. Let's get someone headed your way.

First, a quick safety check: if you smell gas (like rotten eggs) or your carbon monoxide alarm is going off, leave the house now and call 911 or your gas utility from outside.

If you don't smell gas, two quick questions:
1. What's your ZIP code? Then I can look up HVAC companies near you.
2. What is the furnace doing? For example, is it completely dead, or does the fan run but blow cold air? Is it gas, oil or electric? And have you checked the thermostat and the furnace breaker yet?
no gas smell. 94087, it's a gas furnace, fan runs but just blows cold air. already swapped the thermostat batteries, it's set to 70 but house is at 57

Thanks, that helps. A fan that runs but only blows cold air on a gas furnace usually points to an ignition problem: a dirty flame sensor, a failed igniter, a pilot that's out, or a safety switch that tripped (a clogged filter can cause that). A tech can usually figure out which one pretty quickly. In the meantime, check that the furnace filter isn't badly clogged. If it is, swap it out.

One of the outlets in my kitchen sparked and now half the kitchen has no power.

That sounds scary. Here's what to do right now to stay safe:

- Don't plug anything into that outlet or try to reset it. Unplug whatever was plugged in, but only if you can do it without touching the outlet itself.
- If you smell burning, see smoke, or the wall plate feels warm, get everyone out and call 911.
- If you can safely get to your breaker panel, check for a tripped breaker. If one has tripped, leave it off. Turning it back on could make the outlet spark again before an electrician has looked at it.

An electrician is the right pro for this. Two quick questions so I can find someone nearby:

1. What's your ZIP code?
2. Do you smell burning, or do you see scorch marks on the outlet?
It's 94087. No burning smell now, though there's a little dark mark on the outlet cover. I did already try resetting the breaker last night and it tripped again right away, so I've left it off since.

Leaving the breaker off was the right call. If it trips again immediately after a reset, there's probably a short in that outlet or on that circuit, and an electrician needs to look at it before it's used again. Since there's no burning smell and the breaker is off, this doesn't need emergency service, but I'd still try to get someone out within a day.

kitchen sink totally clogged, water won't go down at all

That's a pain, especially with dishes piling up. A fully stopped kitchen drain is usually a grease or food clog in the trap or the branch line, and a plumber can usually snake it out.

Two quick questions so I can find someone nearby:
1. What's your ZIP code?
2. Have you tried anything yet, like a plunger, drain cleaner or running the garbage disposal? And is water backing up into the other sink basin or the dishwasher?

One tip for now: if you've already poured chemical drain cleaner in, tell the plumber, and don't plunge, because it can splash.
94087. Water's standing in both basins since last night, and I already tried a plunger and some Drano. Also the disposal just hums when I flip it on but doesn't spin.

Thanks, that helps. A couple of safety notes first:
- Since there's Drano in that standing water, don't plunge again and keep your hands out of it. It's caustic. Be sure to tell the plumber it's in there.
- The humming means the disposal is jammed or its motor is stalled. Turn its switch off and leave it off, since running it like that can burn out the motor. Never reach into it.

how much does it cost to fix a water heater

I can't give you a price, even a rough one. Water heater repair costs depend a lot on what the technician finds, and the provider will give you a quote. When I send your request, I can add a note saying you want the diagnostic or trip fee and a written quote before any work starts.

What's involved depends on the problem. Some common ones:
- No hot water or it runs out fast: often a heating element or thermostat on electric units, or a pilot, thermocouple or gas valve problem on gas units
- Leaking from the tank itself: usually means the tank needs replacing
- Leaking from fittings or the pressure relief valve: often a smaller fix
- Popping or rumbling sounds: usually sediment buildup, and flushing the tank may help

If you see water pooling near outlets or electrical equipment, or you smell gas, tell me right away. There are safety steps to take first.

To find the right local plumber for you:
1. What's going on with it, and is it gas or electric?
2. What's your ZIP code?
It's gas, about 12 years old, and the water's only been lukewarm since Sunday. There's also a small puddle under it, no gas smell though. ZIP is 94087.

A 12-year-old gas heater with lukewarm water and a small puddle is worth getting looked at soon. Twelve years is near the end of a typical tank's life, so a leak from the tank itself would usually mean replacing it. A leak from a fitting or the relief valve can often be repaired. The lukewarm water could be sediment buildup, a burner or thermocouple problem, or a thermostat or gas valve problem. The technician will figure out which.

Until then:
- Put down towels or a shallow pan and keep anything valuable away from the puddle.
- If the leak gets worse, close the cold water shutoff valve on the pipe going into the top of the heater.
- If you ever smell gas, leave the house and call 911 or your gas utility from outside.
